html:
The Columbian Exchange was the transfer of crops, animals, people and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia that began with the voyage of Christopher Columbus in 1492. For the first time in some ten thousand years, the two halves of the world were in steady contact.

Diseases moved fastest and did the most harm. Smallpox, measles and influenza came from the Old World, where people had lived with them for centuries. In the Americas no one had immunity. Epidemics, along with war and forced labour, cut the Indigenous population by a large majority within about 150 years, and in the Caribbean almost no one survived. Smallpox struck the Aztecs in 1520, in the middle of the Spanish siege.

Food moved the other way and changed diets everywhere:

  • From the Americas: maize, potatoes, sweet potatoes, cassava, tomatoes, chili peppers, cacao and tobacco. The potato reached Europe around 1570 and maize reached China in the 1500s. Both helped populations grow.
  • To the Americas: wheat, rice, sugar cane, coffee, horses, cattle, pigs and sheep. Horses remade life on the North American plains.

Sugar is the darkest link. Sugar plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean needed huge numbers of workers, and with the native population gone, Europeans turned to Africa. The exchange of species and the Atlantic slave trade grew together, and by 1800 far more Africans than Europeans had crossed to the Americas. The colonies of Spanish America and Portuguese Brazil were built on both.
